q: At the Calcutta Congress session (December 1928), the Nehru Report's dominion status goal was accepted, but the Congress issued a one-year ultimatum after which, if unmet, it would:
o: Accept permanent dyarchy
Immediately merge with the Muslim League
Dissolve itself as an organisation
Demand complete independence and launch a civil disobedience movement

q: Lord Irwin's declaration of October 31, 1929 stated that it was implicit in the Declaration of 1917 that India's constitutional progress would culminate in:
o: Immediate complete independence
A unitary British administration
Dominion status, though with no specified timeframe
Permanent dyarchy

q: The Delhi Manifesto (November 2, 1929), issued by prominent national leaders, set which condition regarding the proposed Round Table Conference?
o: That the conference should focus solely on economic issues
That the conference should formulate a constitution to implement dominion status (acting as a constituent assembly) rather than debate whether dominion status should be granted
That the conference should be held in India rather than London
That the Congress should have no representation at the conference

q: The Independence Pledge, read out across India on January 26, 1930 and drafted by Gandhi, committed people to prepare for civil disobedience primarily through:
o: Emigration from British India
Non-payment of taxes and withdrawal of voluntary association from British government
Formation of a parallel legislature
Armed rebellion

q: Gandhi chose salt as the central theme of civil disobedience mainly because:
o: It had no historical significance in Indian life
It affected only urban populations
It linked swaraj to a universal grievance of the rural poor without socially divisive implications, unlike a no-rent campaign
It was the most expensive commodity taxed by the British

q: The raid on Dharasana Salt Works (May 21, 1930), which resulted in a brutal lathi-charge leaving 2 dead and 320 injured, was led by:
o: Rajendra Prasad and C.R. Das
Sarojini Naidu, Imam Sahib and Manilal (Gandhi's son)
Subhash Bose and J.M. Sengupta
Jawaharlal Nehru and Vallabhbhai Patel

q: American journalist Web Miller's eyewitness report of the Dharasana raid, describing the satyagrahis' calm discipline despite being beaten, had which significant effect?
o: It led to immediate British withdrawal from India
It was suppressed and never published
It had no impact on international opinion
It brought international attention and condemnation to British repression in India

q: Which of the following differences between the Civil Disobedience Movement and the Non-Cooperation Movement is correctly identified in the chapter?
o: Muslim participation was far greater in the Civil Disobedience Movement than in Non-Cooperation
Labour unrest was a major coinciding feature of the Civil Disobedience Movement, unlike Non-Cooperation
The Civil Disobedience Movement's stated objective was complete independence, and it involved law violation from the outset, unlike the earlier movement's focus on specific wrongs
The Civil Disobedience Movement saw fewer imprisonments than Non-Cooperation

q: At the Karachi Congress session (March 1931), held just days after the execution of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru, the Congress:
o: Disapproved of political violence while admiring the martyrs' bravery and sacrifice, and endorsed the Gandhi-Irwin Pact
Refused to comment on the executions
Fully endorsed revolutionary violence as a legitimate method
Rejected the Gandhi-Irwin Pact entirely

q: At the Karachi session, the Congress adopted two significant resolutions — on Fundamental Rights and on the National Economic Programme. Which of the following was part of the Fundamental Rights resolution?
o: Right to workers and peasants to form unions
Universal adult franchise and neutrality of the state in religious matters
State ownership of key industries
Reduction in land revenue for peasants

q: The Karachi Resolution's National Economic Programme included proposals such as:
o: Complete privatisation of all industries
Abolition of trade unions
State ownership and control of key industries, mines and means of transport, along with a living wage and limited working hours
Elimination of land revenue reduction demands

q: The outcome of the First Round Table Conference included general agreement that India would develop into a federation, though the conference achieved little because:
o: All parties reached full consensus immediately
Britain granted immediate dominion status, making further talks unnecessary
The Indian National Congress, the primary nationalist voice, was absent, and civil disobedience continued in India
The princely states refused any form of federal participation

q: At the Second Round Table Conference, Gandhi controversially argued that untouchables should NOT be treated as a separate minority because:
o: He supported the Muslim League's position on separate electorates
He wanted to avoid discussing caste altogether
He believed all minorities should be abolished entirely
He considered them to be Hindus, and thus part of the Hindu community rather than a distinct minority

q: The Second Round Table Conference became deadlocked primarily over the question of:
o: The role of the princely states in a future federation
Minority representation, with Muslims, depressed classes, Christians and Anglo-Indians uniting in a 'Minorities' Pact' demanding separate electorates
The location of the next conference
The exact wording of the dominion status declaration

q: At the conclusion of the Second RTC, Ramsay MacDonald announced, among other things, the creation of two new Muslim-majority provinces:
o: Punjab and Bengal
Baluchistan and Kashmir
Assam and Bihar
North-West Frontier Province and Sindh

q: The Third Round Table Conference (November-December 1932) differed from the previous two mainly in that:
o: It was attended by all major Congress leaders
It resulted in the immediate implementation of dominion status
It achieved full consensus on India's constitutional future
It was not attended by the Indian National Congress or Gandhi, and was largely ignored by most Indian leaders

q: The second phase of Civil Disobedience (1932-1934) was marked by intense government repression sometimes described as a form of:
o: A negotiated ceasefire with the Congress
Complete government inaction
'Civil Martial Law' — repressive ordinances amounting to virtual martial law under civilian control
Full restoration of civil liberties

q: The Communal Award, announced by Ramsay MacDonald on August 16, 1932, was based on the findings of which committee?
o: The Hunter Committee
The Simon Commission
The Indian Franchise Committee (Lothian Committee)
The Nehru Committee

q: Under the Communal Award, how many reserved seats were granted to the depressed classes?
o: Seventy-eight
Fifty
Twenty
One hundred

q: Gandhi's principal objection to the Communal Award's treatment of the depressed classes was that:
o: He wanted the depressed classes to have fewer reserved seats
He believed the depressed classes deserved no representation at all
He supported separate electorates for all minorities except the depressed classes
Treating them as a separate political entity would undermine the campaign to abolish untouchability, keeping untouchables 'untouchable in perpetuity'

q: The Poona Pact, signed by B.R. Ambedkar on behalf of the depressed classes on September 24, 1932, resulted in:
o: Continuation of separate electorates with fewer reserved seats
Extension of separate electorates to all Hindu sub-castes
Abandonment of separate electorates for depressed classes, but an increase in reserved seats from 71 to 147 in provincial legislatures
Complete removal of any reserved seats for depressed classes

q: Which of the following is identified in the chapter as a negative long-term impact of the Poona Pact on the depressed classes?
o: It made depressed class representatives vulnerable to being chosen as compliant 'stooges' by caste Hindu organisations under joint electorates
It granted complete political independence to the depressed classes from caste Hindu influence
It eliminated the need for any future reservation policy
It gave depressed classes a separate, sovereign political existence

q: Gandhi's approach to caste and untouchability differed from Ambedkar's in that Gandhi:
o: Refused to engage with the issue of untouchability at all
Also sought complete annihilation of the caste system, agreeing fully with Ambedkar
Distinguished between abolishing untouchability and abolishing the caste system itself, whereas Ambedkar sought annihilation of the caste system entirely
Believed untouchability was sanctioned by scripture and should be preserved

q: Regarding methods of political and social change, which of the following correctly distinguishes Gandhi's and Ambedkar's approaches?
o: Both leaders relied exclusively on parliamentary methods
Gandhi favoured strict legalism while Ambedkar favoured mass civil disobedience
Both leaders rejected the use of law entirely in favour of direct action
Gandhi relied on persuasion, morality and civil disobedience against unjust laws, while Ambedkar favoured legal and constitutional methods within the framework of law

q: Regarding views on democracy and governance, which best captures the Gandhi-Ambedkar difference?
o: Gandhi favoured strong centralised parliamentary rule, while Ambedkar opposed all forms of representative government
Neither leader expressed any views on the nature of democratic governance
Both leaders were equally enthusiastic supporters of parliamentary democracy

Ambedkar favoured a parliamentary system and mass democracy as pressure on government, while Gandhi had limited respect for parliamentary systems, fearing mass democracy could lead to domination by leaders

q: Regarding the relationship between religion and untouchability, Ambedkar's position (in his later years) differed from Gandhi's in that Ambedkar:
o: Believed Hinduism required no reform whatsoever
Refused to discuss the relationship between religion and caste at all
Ultimately denounced Hinduism as unreformable and later left it, while Gandhi maintained that caste had nothing inherently to do with Hindu religious precepts
Agreed entirely with Gandhi that untouchability was unrelated to Hindu scripture

q: Justice Krishna Iyer's assessment of Gandhi and Ambedkar, quoted in the chapter, suggests that:
o: Ambedkar was entirely dependent on Gandhi's guidance
Both shared a common opposition to social evil and imperial injustice, though a fundamental difference — more apparent than real — separated their approaches
The two leaders had no common ground whatsoever
Gandhi fully endorsed all of Ambedkar's constitutional proposals
